es: Responder por escrito y en tiempo limitado a una pregunta sorpresa con frase para ganar tiempo, postura firme, razón, ejemplo y cierre, sin quedarte a medias ni sentarte en la valla.

teaching.en: A surprise question tests whether you can think on your feet, so buy a second and name your topic at once.
teaching.es: Una pregunta sorpresa comprueba si puedes improvisar, así que gana un segundo y nombra tu tema enseguida.
teaching.explanationEs: Surprise question: pregunta inesperada; la estructura te salva.

teaching.en: If you sit on the fence, the listener hears only doubt, so pick a stance and commit to it.
teaching.es: Si no tomas partido, el oyente solo oye dudas, así que elige una postura y comprométete con ella.
teaching.explanationEs: Sit on the fence = no tomar partido; commit to se construye con to.

doubt, so pick a stance and commit to it.

teaching.en: In the end, it boils down to this: a specialist goes deep into one field, while a generalist moves easily between several.
teaching.es: En el fondo, todo se reduce a esto: un especialista profundiza en un campo, mientras que un generalista se mueve con facilidad entre varios.
teaching.explanationEs: It boils down to introduce la esencia de una comparación.

teaching.en: One vivid example can tip the balance in a one-minute answer, provided that it stays close to the topic.
teaching.es: Un ejemplo vívido puede inclinar la balanza en una respuesta de un minuto, siempre que se mantenga cerca del tema.
teaching.explanationEs: Tip the balance = hacer que algo se incline hacia un lado.

teaching.en: Working against the clock in a surprise round puts you on the spot, so keep ten seconds for your close.
teaching.es: Trabajar contra reloj en una ronda sorpresa te pone en el acto a prueba, así que reserva diez segundos para el cierre.
teaching.explanationEs: Con poco tiempo, reserva los últimos segundos para el cierre.

teaching.en: A clear stance is worth more than a perfect answer: listeners forgive a rough phrase far sooner than a missing opinion.
teaching.es: Una postura clara vale más que una respuesta perfecta: los oyentes perdonan una frase torpe antes que la falta de una opinión.
teaching.explanationEs: Elegir pronto evita divagar y da estructura al resto del minuto.

prompt.es: Completa: «Mi postura es que las oficinas todavía importan.»

feedback.es: My stance is that… declara tu postura desde el primer momento de la respuesta.

hint.es: Es el sustantivo de la lista que significa postura.

origin.text: Asked about remote work, she replied, “That's a tricky one, but my ___ is that offices still matter.”

prompt.es: Ordena: «Es mejor comprometerse con una postura que quedarse indeciso.»

answer.text: It is better to commit to a stance than to sit on the fence

feedback.es: Commit to a stance contrasta con sit on the fence: comprometerse frente a no tomar partido.

hint.es: Comparación con better… than…; commit va seguido de to.

prompt.es: ¿Qué frase gana tiempo y se compromete a la vez con una postura?

choices.text: That's a tricky one, but my stance is that a village suits families.
That's a tricky one, and honestly both places have advantages and some disadvantages too.
That's a tricky one, so perhaps you could answer it for me first, please.

feedback.es: La que gana tiempo con «a tricky one» y se compromete con una postura; las otras se sientan en la valla o no contestan.

hint.es: Busca la que hace las dos cosas: valora la pregunta y toma postura.

origin.text: The host has asked whether it is better to live in a village or in a city, and you have only sixty seconds. You want to start with a sentence that buys time and commits at once.

feedback.es: Commit to significa comprometerse con algo, y watch the clock recuerda vigilar el tiempo.

sentences: I would ___ to one stance in the first ten seconds.
Watch the ___ so that you can close on time.

prompt.es: Escucha la respuesta de un minuto y elige cuál es su ejemplo.

choices.text: Code shaping almost every job in almost every modern company.
A nurse who built a small tool that tracks supplies.
Coding being worth learning for absolutely everyone who works today.

feedback.es: El ejemplo es el caso concreto de la tía enfermera; lo que dice sobre los empleos es la razón y la última frase es el cierre.

origin.audio: That's a tricky one, but my stance is yes. The main reason is that code shapes almost every job today. For example, my aunt, a nurse, built a small tool that tells her ward when supplies are running low. So, in short, coding is worth learning even if you never work in technology.

prompt.es: ¿Qué cierre es mejor para una respuesta de un minuto?

choices.text: And one more thing, my neighbour also has a cat and a very loud dog.
Well, that is what I think, but to be honest I am not sure about it.
In short, I would choose to be a generalist, because it keeps more doors open.

feedback.es: Un buen cierre resume tu postura en una frase; las otras abren un desvío o muestran inseguridad.

origin.text: You have ten seconds left. You have already given your stance, a reason and an example, and now you need one closing sentence that leaves a clear impression.

prompt.es: Responde a la pregunta sorpresa en un minuto, con las cuatro partes.

answer.text: That's a tricky one, so let me think for a second. My stance is that a generalist has more options than a specialist. The main reason is that jobs change faster than any single specialist can follow. A generalist can move between fields, learn new tools and adapt when a company changes direction. For example, my cousin trained as a nurse, then worked in a hospital office, and now manages a small clinic. If she had stayed only a specialist, she would not have had those chances. Of course, specialists are important, and I would not want a generalist to be my doctor. Sorry, I'm rambling a little; let me get back to my point. In the end, it boils down to this: you want a specialist when lives are at stake and a generalist when the ground keeps moving. So, in short, I would rather be a generalist with one strong skill, because that mix gives me both skill and choices.
accepted: That's a tricky one, so let me think for a second. My stance is that a generalist has more options than a specialist. The main reason is that jobs change faster than any single specialist can follow. A generalist can move between fields, learn new tools and adapt when a company changes direction. For example, my cousin trained as a nurse, then worked in a hospital office, and now manages a small clinic. If she had stayed only a specialist, she would not have had those chances. Of course, specialists are important, and I would not want a generalist to be my doctor. Sorry, I'm rambling a little; let me get back to my point. In the end, it boils down to this: you want a specialist when lives are at stake and a generalist when the ground keeps moving. So, in short, I would rather be a generalist with one strong skill, because that mix gives me both skill and choices.

Let me think for a moment. I would say that specialists are better, so my stance is clear. The first reason is that experts solve hard problems faster. A specialist has spent years on one subject, and companies pay more for that skill. For example, my uncle is an engineer who only repairs bridges, and he is always busy because nobody else can do his job. Some people say that a generalist is more flexible, and that is true. However, I think being flexible without real skill is risky, because a generalist may never learn anything well. That is why I prefer to commit to one field and to learn it thoroughly. To sum up, I believe that a specialist has the advantage, and I would advise young people to choose one area and to become really good at it.

feedback.es: Una respuesta de un minuto gana tiempo, declara la postura, la justifica con razón y ejemplo, y cierra con una síntesis.

origin.text: Pregunta sorpresa: «¿Es mejor ser especialista o generalista?» Escribe 220–280 palabras: una frase para ganar tiempo, tu postura, una razón, un ejemplo y un cierre (puedes reparar un desvío).

evidenceGroups: off the top of my head

prompt.es: Escucha el comentario de la entrenadora y elige qué da a entender sobre la respuesta.

choices.text: That managing the minute matters as much as the ideas themselves.
That an extra example is always worth the risk of running out of time.
That the student's problem was hesitation at the start of her answer.
That a closing sentence matters more than the main reason does.

feedback.es: Al señalar el reloj en lugar de criticar el contenido, da a entender que la gestión del tiempo pesa tanto como la calidad de las ideas.

origin.audio: After the timer stopped, the coach played back a student's answer. The student had begun well: a short pause, then a clear stance on whether the school day should start later. The reason was convincing, and the example, about her brother falling asleep in his first lesson, was vivid. But with ten seconds left she remembered a second example and began telling it, and the minute ended before she could close. The coach did not question the content. She pointed at the clock and said that an answer without a closing sentence is like a story without its last line.

prompt.es: ¿Qué punto débil señala este comentario sobre la respuesta cronometrada?

choices.text: That her reasons were convincing but her example came too late in the minute.
That conceding so much hurt the stance she had taken first.
That the opposing view should have been ignored completely to sound convinced.
That she spent too long on the reason and skipped the close.

feedback.es: Dice que se comprometió al principio, pero luego enumeró ventajas de ambos lados: el oyente no sabe qué elegiría, así que concedió demasiado y debilitó su postura.

origin.text: Feedback on your timed answer: you committed to your stance in the first sentence, which I liked, but then you sat on the fence for the rest, listing advantages on both sides. A listener cannot tell what you would actually choose. Next time, concede the opposing view in a single clause and spend the remaining time defending your own.

prompt.es: Completa: «Todo se reduce a si el trabajo exige una habilidad profunda o varias.»

feedback.es: It boils down to introduce la esencia de una comparación: aquí, profundidad frente a amplitud.

origin.text: Both matter, but in the end, it boils ___ to whether the work needs one deep skill or many small ones.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Un ejemplo vívido puede inclinar la balanza en un minuto.»

answer.text: One vivid example can tip the balance in a minute

feedback.es: Tip the balance significa inclinar la balanza: un buen ejemplo decide la respuesta.

prompt.es: ¿Qué sugiere la decisión del juez sobre lo que valora en una respuesta?

choices.text: That a longer answer is always better than a shorter one.
That speaker B won mainly because he used sharper vocabulary.
That a committed stance counts for more than a neutral answer.
That a judge prefers speakers who avoid taking sides.

feedback.es: El juez elige a quien se compromete con una postura y no a quien se queda en el «depende»: valora el compromiso por encima de la neutralidad.

origin.text: In the debating club's final round, speaker A said, “I suppose both are fine; it depends on the person.” Speaker B said, “My stance is that specialists win, because companies pay for real skill.” B gave one sharp example and closed in a sentence. The judge voted for B without hesitation.

prompt.es: Escribe la frase de cierre: «En resumen, prefiero ser especialista en una sola área.»

answer.text: So, in short, I would rather be a specialist in one area.
accepted: So, in short, I would rather be a specialist in one area.
In short, I prefer to be a specialist in one field.
To sum up, I would rather be a specialist in one area.
In short, I would rather be a specialist in one field.
In conclusion, I would rather specialise in one area.

feedback.es: El cierre repite la postura en una frase breve con so, in short o to sum up.

origin.text: Cierra la respuesta con una frase breve: «En resumen, prefiero ser especialista en una sola área.»
